beginner: Pomegranate is famously easy about soil. It grows best in a deep loam but will handle sandy soils and even heavy clay, as long as water drains away and does not sit around the roots. It also shrugs off alkaline (high-pH) and mildly salty soils that bother most fruit. The one thing it will not take is soggy ground: constantly wet roots bring on root rot. If your soil is heavy or drainage is poor, plant on a raised mound or bed so the roots stay above the wet.
seasoned: Pomegranate is one of the most soil-adaptable fruits: it prefers a deep loam but tolerates sandy soils, heavy clay, alkaline pH, and mild salinity that would stunt most fruit trees. Drainage is the one firm requirement, since waterlogged soil invites root rot (including Armillaria on wet, heavy ground). On clay or low sites, plant on a raised berm or bed to lift the crown above standing water. It needs little organic matter and thrives on lean ground.

beginner: Pomegranate grows well in a wide pH range, about 5.5 to 7.0, and tolerates up to around 7.2 (pH just measures how acidic or alkaline the soil is). It is unusually easygoing about alkaline soil, so most gardeners never need to adjust pH for it. Test your soil before planting, and only correct if it is far outside that range.
seasoned: Pomegranate does well across a broad pH band, roughly 5.5 to 7.0, and tolerates up to about 7.2. It is notably alkaline-tolerant, so pH is seldom a limiting factor and rarely needs amending. Test before planting and correct only if the soil is well outside the tolerated range.

beginner: Pomegranate does not need much feeding. In late winter or early spring, scatter a small amount of balanced fertilizer around the plant and water it in. Do not overdo nitrogen (the first number on the bag), because too much grows leaves and base shoots instead of fruit. On poor or sandy soil, a light second feeding in late spring helps a young plant, but an established one usually needs very little.
seasoned: Pomegranate is a light feeder. Broadcast a modest amount of balanced fertilizer around the root zone in late winter to early spring as growth begins, and water it in. Avoid heavy nitrogen: excess N drives vegetative growth and suckering at the expense of flowers and fruit, and can worsen soft, split-prone fruit. On lean or sandy soils a light second feeding in late spring helps young plants; established plants often need little or none.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is plenty for a pomegranate. Go light, and especially do not overdo the first number, nitrogen, which grows leaves and shoots instead of fruit.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits pomegranate; it is a light feeder and draws modestly on all three nutrients. Keep nitrogen restrained, since excess pushes suckers and soft growth over flowering and fruit set.

beginner: Feed lightly. A simple approach is a small handful of 10-10-10 for each foot of the plant's height, spread around the plant in late winter, and no more than that for a full-grown one. Do not fertilize right when you plant; wait until it starts growing. If the plant is already growing strongly with deep green leaves, feed less or skip it.
seasoned: A light hand is the rule. A common home approach is about 1 to 2 ounces of actual nitrogen per year of plant age in the early years (for example, a modest handful of 10-10-10 per foot of height), capped for a mature plant, applied in late winter. Skip feeding at planting; wait until growth begins. If growth is already vigorous and green, feed less or not at all.

beginner: Pomegranate is self-fruitful, so one plant makes fruit on its own and you do not need a second plant to pollinate it (though a second pomegranate nearby can improve fruit set a little). For a shrub like this, the things that help are not the usual vegetable-garden pairings but the space around it: keep grass and weeds pulled back from the base so they do not compete with a young plant, and give it an open, sunny, breezy spot, because crowded, still, humid air at bloom makes flowers drop instead of setting fruit. Flowering plants nearby that draw bees can help set, and they bring in helpful insects that keep aphids and whiteflies down.
seasoned: Pomegranate is self-fruitful, so a single plant sets a crop on its own (a second plant nearby can modestly improve set). The interactions that matter for this shrub are about air, light, and the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared from the base so they do not compete with a young plant, and site it in open, sunny, breezy ground, since crowded, humid, still air at bloom causes flowers to abort. Nearby pollinator plantings aid set and recruit the beneficials that hold aphids, whiteflies, and mealybugs in check.

beginner: Usually you see nothing wrong on the outside of the fruit, because the damage is inside. If you cut a fruit open, you find brown spots on the inner skin and seeds (arils) that have gone dark, shriveled, or corky. It is worst late in the season as the fruit ripens, and it can let rot start inside.
seasoned: Often no external mark on the fruit at all; the damage is inside. Cut a fed-on fruit and you find brown spots on the inner rind where the insect's needlelike mouthpart pierced, and arils that have darkened, withered, or turned corky. Late-season feeding as fruit ripens is the worst, and it opens the door to internal fungal rots.

beginner: A big brown bug called the leaf-footed bug, named for the little leaf-shaped flares on its back legs. It and its young pierce the fruit to feed, and that can carry in yeasts and fungi that discolor and rot the seeds inside. The adults spend winter hidden in sheltered groups, then move onto the fruit as it forms.
seasoned: The leaf-footed bug (Leptoglossus species), a large brown true bug with flattened, leaf-like flares on its hind legs. Adults and nymphs pierce fruit to feed; on pomegranate their feeding can introduce yeasts and fungal spores that discolor and rot the arils. They overwinter as adults in sheltered aggregations and move onto fruit as it develops.

beginner: For a backyard plant, the best fixes are hands-on: in the cool early morning, knock the bugs into a bucket of soapy water, and clean up the weedy, sheltered places where they spend the winter and gather. Where you can, cover fruit clusters with fine mesh bags. Flowers nearby that bring in helpful insects also keep numbers down.
seasoned: There is no easy rescue spray for a backyard plant. The practical controls are physical: hand-pick or knock adults and nymphs into soapy water in the cool early morning when they are sluggish, clear the weedy and sheltered spots where they overwinter and aggregate, and bag developing fruit clusters in mesh where feasible. Encourage the natural egg parasites and general predators by keeping insectary flowers nearby.

beginner: Keep an eye out from the time fruit forms, because you cannot see the damage from outside until you cut a fruit open. Keep weeds cleared to take away the places the bugs hide and breed, and look for the adults gathering in spring. Catching and removing them early, before there are many, works best.
seasoned: Monitor from fruit set onward, since the internal damage is invisible until you cut the fruit. Keep the area weed-free to remove overwintering and breeding habitat, and watch for the adults congregating in spring. Early detection and hand-removal before populations build is the most effective home strategy.

beginner: Groups of tiny soft insects on new shoots and the undersides of leaves, leaving a sticky coating (honeydew) that turns into black sooty mold, plus curled new leaves and ants running up and down the plant.
seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on new shoots, leaf undersides, and flower stems, with sticky honeydew, sooty black mold on leaves and fruit, curled or distorted new growth, and attending ants.

beginner: Aphids, tiny sap-sucking insects that build up on soft new growth in spring. They multiply quickly, and the sticky honeydew they leave grows black mold and attracts ants that guard them.
seasoned: Several aphid species colonize tender pomegranate growth in spring, multiplying fast in warm weather. Their honeydew supports sooty mold and draws ants, which protect the aphids from predators.

beginner: Spraying the plant with a strong stream of water knocks most aphids off and is often all an established plant needs. Let the good bugs (ladybugs, lacewings) do their job by avoiding harsh sprays; insecticidal soap helps if there are a lot. Keeping ants off the plant lets the helpful insects control them.
seasoned: A strong jet of water knocks aphids off and is often enough on an established plant. Preserve natural enemies (ladybugs, lacewings, syrphid larvae) by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays; insecticidal soap or horticultural oil handles heavier infestations. Control ants, which farm aphids, to let predators work.

beginner: Do not overfeed with nitrogen, because all that soft new growth attracts aphids. Grow flowers nearby to bring in helpful insects, and keep ants away so those helpers can do their work.
seasoned: Keep nitrogen feeding moderate, since lush growth pushed by excess nitrogen draws aphids. Support beneficial insects with nearby flowers, and manage ants so predators are not chased off.

beginner: Tiny white insects like little moths that flutter up when you brush the plant, sitting under the leaves along with their flat, pale young. They leave sticky honeydew and black sooty mold, and a lot of them yellow the leaves.
seasoned: Tiny white moth-like insects that fly up in clouds when the plant is disturbed, gathered on leaf undersides with their pale nymphs; honeydew and sooty mold follow, and heavy infestations yellow and weaken leaves.

beginner: Whiteflies, small sap-sucking insects that live under the leaves and multiply fast in warm weather. Like aphids, they leave honeydew that grows sooty mold.
seasoned: Whiteflies, small sap-feeding insects that colonize leaf undersides and reproduce rapidly in warm weather. Like aphids, they excrete honeydew that fosters sooty mold.

beginner: Spray the leaves with water and let helpful insects do most of the work; they usually keep whiteflies under control outdoors. Insecticidal soap sprayed under the leaves helps if there are many, and yellow sticky cards catch the adults.
seasoned: Hose off foliage and rely on natural enemies (lacewings, ladybugs, parasitic wasps), which usually keep whiteflies in check on an outdoor plant. Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on leaf undersides helps in heavy cases; yellow sticky traps monitor and reduce adults.

beginner: Keep the plant healthy, avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, and do not let it get dusty and stressed, which whiteflies like. Avoid harsh sprays so the helpful insects survive.
seasoned: Keep plants healthy and avoid excess nitrogen and dusty, stressed conditions that favor whitefly buildup. Preserve natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides.

beginner: Fuzzy white cottony spots (mealybugs) tucked into branch joints and inside the crown of the fruit, or small hard brown bumps (scale) stuck to stems and leaves. Both leave sticky honeydew and black mold, and mealybugs hiding in the fruit crown can get inside the fruit.
seasoned: Cottony white tufts (mealybugs) in leaf axils, branch crotches, and inside the fruit calyx (crown), or small immobile brown or waxy bumps (scale) on stems and leaves; both produce honeydew and sooty mold, and mealybugs hidden in the crown can contaminate the fruit interior.

beginner: Mealybugs and scale insects, sap-sucking pests that hide in sheltered spots, including the crown of the fruit. Ants move them around and protect them, and their honeydew grows black mold.
seasoned: Mealybugs and various scale insects, slow-moving or immobile sap feeders that shelter in protected spots including the fruit's crown. Ants tend and spread them, and their honeydew fuels sooty mold.

beginner: Wipe visible mealybugs with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol, spray with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap, and cut out badly infested branches. Keep ants off so the helpful insects can work, and throw away any fruit with bugs packed into the crown.
seasoned: Spot-treat with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap, dab visible mealybug colonies with an alcohol-dipped swab, and prune out heavily infested wood. Control ants to let natural enemies (including mealybug destroyers and parasitic wasps) suppress them. Remove fruit with infested crowns.

beginner: Keep ants away, do not overfeed, and check the fruit crowns and branch joints where these pests hide. An open, airy plant with good light bothers them.
seasoned: Keep ants under control, avoid excess nitrogen, and inspect the fruit crown and branch crotches where these pests hide. Good airflow and light through the canopy discourage them.

beginner: From the outside the fruit looks almost fine, maybe a bit light or a paler red, but inside it is rotting: the seeds turn brown and mushy with black mold. There is usually no sign on the outside, so you only find it when you cut the fruit open.
seasoned: The fruit looks nearly normal outside, perhaps a little light in weight or slightly off-color (a paler red), while the interior rots: arils turn brown and mushy and a black mold sporulates inside. There is often no external cue, so the rot is discovered only on cutting.

beginner: A fungus called Alternaria gets into the fruit through the open flower in damp, rainy bloom weather and grows quietly inside. Wounds from insects (like the leaf-footed bug) or birds let it in too. Wet weather around bloom is the main cause, so it is worse in humid areas.
seasoned: The fungus Alternaria (and related molds) infects through the open flower during rainy or humid bloom weather and grows silently inside the developing fruit. Insect and bird punctures (notably leaf-footed bug feeding) give it a second way in. Wet weather at and after bloom is the main driver, which is why it is a bigger problem in humid climates.

beginner: Once a fruit is rotting inside, it cannot be saved. The way to fight it is to prevent it: it is much less of a problem in hot, dry weather, so keep the leaf-footed bug and other fruit-piercing pests under control, keep the plant open and airy, and pick off and throw away any rotted or old dried fruit so the mold does not spread to next year.
seasoned: There is no cure once the inside is rotting; the fruit is lost. Control is preventive: it is far less of a problem in hot, dry climates, so the main levers are managing leaf-footed bug and other fruit-piercing pests, keeping the canopy open and airy, and removing and destroying infected and mummified fruit so spores do not carry over.

beginner: Grow it where summers are hot and dry if you can, keep the plant open, and water at the ground rather than over the top. Keep fruit-piercing bugs in check, clean up rotted and old dried fruit, and know that in humid, rainy areas this disease may limit your crop, so pick the most open, breezy spot.
seasoned: Favor dry-climate siting, open canopies, and drip (not overhead) watering to keep bloom and fruit dry. Control fruit-piercing insects, sanitize by removing mummies and rotted fruit, and, in humid regions, expect this to be a limiting disease and choose the most open, breezy sites.

beginner: Fuzzy gray-brown mold on the flowers and fruit, often starting at the crown end or a wound, with soft brown rot that spreads in cool, damp weather and in storage. It can spread from one fruit to another where they touch.
seasoned: Fuzzy gray-brown mold on flowers, on fruit (often starting at the crown or a wound), and on stored fruit; soft brown rot spreads in cool, wet, or humid conditions and in storage, and can move between touching fruit.

beginner: A fungus called Botrytis, or gray mold, that infects flowers and damaged or overripe fruit in cool, damp weather. It survives on old fruit and plant litter and is a common cause of rot in stored fruit.
seasoned: The fungus Botrytis cinerea (gray mold), which infects flowers and wounded or overripe fruit in cool, wet, humid conditions. It overwinters on plant debris and old fruit and is a common cause of post-harvest rot.

beginner: Pick off and throw away moldy flowers, fruit, and litter right away. Keep the plant open and dry, pick before the rains, handle fruit gently so it does not bruise, and refrigerate good fruit soon, since cold slows the mold. Once a fruit is rotting there is no home spray that fixes it.
seasoned: Remove and destroy moldy flowers, fruit, and debris promptly. Keep the canopy open and dry, harvest before rains, handle fruit gently to avoid wounds, and refrigerate sound fruit quickly, since cold storage slows the mold. There is no home spray cure once fruit is rotting.

beginner: Keep the plant open and the leaves dry: prune for airflow, water at the ground, clean up old fruit and litter, and handle and chill fruit carefully at harvest. Remove split or damaged fruit, which is where the mold gets in.
seasoned: Prioritize air circulation and dry foliage: open pruning, root-zone watering, prompt sanitation of old fruit and debris, and gentle handling with quick cooling at harvest. Cull split and wounded fruit, which are entry points.

beginner: Small dark spots on the fruit and leaves that grow and run together; badly spotted fruit looks rough and russeted, and heavy leaf spotting yellows the leaves and drops them. It is worst in warm, humid, rainy areas.
seasoned: Small dark spots and blotches on fruit and leaves that enlarge and merge; heavily spotted fruit is russeted and downgraded, and severe leaf infection causes yellowing and drop. Most common and damaging in warm, humid, rainy climates.

beginner: A fungus (Cercospora punicae, along with related fungi in the same wet climates) that spreads when leaves and fruit stay wet for a long time. It is a big reason pomegranate does poorly in the humid Southeast and other rainy places.
seasoned: The fungus Cercospora punicae (with related fungi such as Colletotrichum and Botryosphaeria in the same wet climates). It thrives on prolonged leaf and fruit wetness, so it is a leading reason pomegranate fruits poorly in the humid Southeast and other rainy regions.

beginner: There is no easy home cure, so prevention matters: plant in an open, sunny, breezy spot so the leaves dry quickly, prune to open the plant, water at the ground, and clean up fallen leaves and spotted fruit. In damp, rainy climates this disease will likely limit your fruit quality no matter what.
seasoned: Home control is limited and preventive: choose an open, sunny, breezy site so foliage dries fast, prune for airflow, water at the ground, and remove fallen leaves and infected fruit. In consistently humid, rainy climates, expect this disease to cap fruit quality regardless of care.

beginner: The best defense is where and how you plant it: an open, breezy, sloped spot with good air movement, wide spacing, an open plant, watering at the ground, and cleaning up fallen leaves and fruit. In hot, dry climates it is barely a problem.
seasoned: Site selection is the main defense: open, sloped, breezy ground with strong air movement, especially at bloom. Wide spacing, open canopies, ground-level irrigation, and sanitation of fallen debris reduce pressure. In hot, dry climates it is a minor issue.

beginner: Water deeply and regularly through spring and summer, then cut back in winter. A young plant needs steady water to get established. An older plant can take drought but makes much better fruit with regular deep watering, about once a week in summer heat, more or less depending on your soil and the weather. The most important thing is to keep the water STEADY once the fruit is forming: letting it go dry and then soaking it (or the first fall rains) is what makes pomegranates split. In winter, when the plant is resting, it needs very little.
seasoned: Water deeply and regularly through the growing season, then ease off. Young plants need steady moisture to establish; bearing plants are drought-tolerant but crop far better with regular deep watering, roughly weekly in summer heat, adjusted for soil and weather. The critical discipline is CONSISTENCY from fruit set through ripening: a dry spell followed by heavy water (or the first fall rains) is what splits the fruit. In winter dormancy, water need drops sharply and rainfall usually suffices.

beginner: Each watering should soak the soil deeply down to the roots, not just wet the top. During the fruiting season, aim for about an inch of water a week, more when it is very hot, given as deep, even soaks. Keeping the moisture steady from the time fruit forms until harvest is what stops the fruit from cracking, so avoid letting it dry out and then flooding it.
seasoned: Water deeply enough to wet the full root zone each time rather than sprinkling the surface. Through the fruiting season aim for the rough equivalent of an inch of water per week, more in extreme heat, delivered as deep, even soaks. Steady soil moisture from set to harvest is what prevents splitting; the goal is even, never a dry-then-flood swing.

beginner: Water the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, out to the edge of the branches. What matters most is deep, even watering, because steady moisture is what keeps the fruit from splitting. A layer of mulch helps hold moisture even; just keep it off the trunks.
seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose out toward the canopy edge, keeping the base broad and even. Pomegranate tolerates overhead water better than stone fruit, but even, deep root-zone irrigation is what delivers the consistent moisture that prevents fruit split. Mulch to buffer soil-moisture swings, keeping mulch off the trunks.

beginner: Too much water, or soil that drains poorly, shows up as yellow leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and a plant going downhill, because soaked roots cannot breathe and start to rot. Soil that stays wet all the time is your warning. Pomegranate likes steady moisture but not a swamp.
seasoned: Overwatering and poor drainage show as yellowing leaves, wilting in wet soil, and a declining plant, since waterlogged roots suffocate. Chronically wet, heavy soil invites Armillaria and other root rots, which are hard to reverse. Soil that never dries between waterings is the warning sign; pomegranate wants moisture but not a saturated root zone.

beginner: Too little water shows as wilting, dull or yellow leaves, leaves dropping early, and small fruit. The worst result comes from uneven water: a plant that gets dry and is then watered heavily (or hit by fall rain) will crack its fruit. Try to keep the water steady so this does not happen.
seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting, dull or yellowing leaves, early leaf drop, and small, poorly filled fruit. The most costly symptom is inconsistent water: a drought-stressed plant that is then rewetted, or catches the fall rains, splits its fruit. Catch dry stress before the fruit pays for it.

beginner: While the plant is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps it grow the deep roots it needs.
seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never waterlogged. Deep soaks once or twice a week, adjusted for heat and rain, build the deep, drought-ready root system pomegranate relies on later.

beginner: Once the fruit is forming and filling, keep the water steady. Aim for about an inch a week as deep soaks. This is exactly when even watering keeps the fruit from cracking.
seasoned: From fruit set through ripening, hold the moisture STEADY. Aim for about an inch of water per week as deep, even soaks. This is the window where consistent water prevents splitting and irregular water causes it.

beginner: After the leaves drop and the plant rests for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water in long dry stretches. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.
seasoned: Once the plant drops its leaves and goes dormant, water need falls sharply; rely mostly on rainfall and water only during prolonged dry spells. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.

beginner: Give deep soaks at the ground (a drip line or soaker hose is ideal) and keep the water steady from the time fruit forms until you pick, since even watering is what stops the fruit from splitting. Young plants need regular water for their first couple of years. Older plants handle dry spells but make much better fruit with regular deep watering.
seasoned: Water deeply at the root zone, ideally by drip or soaker, and keep it EVEN from fruit set to harvest; consistency, not volume, is what prevents split fruit. Young plants need steady moisture through their first two seasons to establish; mature plants are strongly drought-tolerant but size and hold fruit far better with regular deep water.

beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to the outdoors) does not apply to pomegranate. You plant it as a dormant bare-root or potted plant in late winter or early spring, not as a tender seedling started inside, so there is nothing to ease outdoors.
seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to pomegranate. It is set out as a dormant bare-root or cutting-grown plant in late winter to early spring, not raised from a tender seedling indoors, so there is no transplant to acclimate.

beginner: Plant a dormant bare-root or potted pomegranate in late winter or early spring, after the worst cold and once the ground can be dug. Soak bare roots in water for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots and set the plant at the same depth it grew before. Unlike a peach, a pomegranate is on its own roots with no graft joint to worry about. Decide now whether you want a bush with several trunks or a single small tree, and cut the plant back a bit to start it. If your soil is heavy or wet, plant on a raised mound. Fill in with the soil you dug out, water it well, and add mulch.
seasoned: Plant a dormant bare-root or cutting-grown pomegranate in late winter to early spring, after the hardest freezes have passed and once the ground can be worked. Soak bare roots for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots and set the plant at the depth it grew in the nursery; because pomegranate is on its own roots (not grafted), there is no graft union to keep above grade. Decide the form at planting, multi-stem shrub or trained tree, and head the plant back to start it. On heavy or wet ground, plant on a raised mound. Backfill with native soil, water in well, and mulch.

beginner: Use a good, fast-draining potting mix made for shrubs or citrus. Pomegranate is not fussy, but it must not sit in soggy mix, so pick one that drains freely. A bark-based mix with some perlite or pumice works well. Do not use heavy garden soil in a pot, since it packs down and stays wet.
seasoned: Use a free-draining container mix (a bark-based blend with perlite or pumice, or a citrus/shrub mix). Pomegranate is easygoing but will not tolerate a waterlogged mix against the crown, so porosity matters more than richness. Avoid heavy native soil, which compacts under frequent irrigation.

seasoned: Keep amendments drainage-first: add perlite or pumice if the base mix is water-retentive, and top-dress lightly with compost rather than blending heavy organics throughout. Skip moisture-retentive additives, which work against the drainage this drought-adapted plant prefers.

beginner: A pomegranate in a pot dries out faster than one in the ground, so check it often in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until water runs out the bottom. Even so, try to keep the watering STEADY once fruit forms, because uneven water splits the fruit even in a pot. Never let the pot stand in a saucer of water, which rots the roots. In winter, water just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.

beginner: Pomegranate is cold-tender, and roots in a pot freeze more easily than roots in the ground. In zones colder than about 8, before hard freezes come, move the pot into an unheated but sheltered spot (a garage, shed, or against a warm wall) that stays cold enough to keep the plant dormant but out of the deep freeze. The plant still needs its winter rest, so do not bring it into a warm, heated room. In mild-winter areas you can leave it outside.
seasoned: Because pomegranate is frost-tender and a container root ball sits several zones colder than open ground, protect potted plants in zones colder than roughly 8. Before hard freezes, move the pot to an unheated but sheltered space (garage, shed, or a warm south wall) that holds dormancy without deep lows, or sink the pot to its rim in a bed and mulch heavily. Do not overwinter it in heated indoor warmth, which breaks dormancy prematurely. In mild-winter regions no protection is needed.

Start with a dwarf variety like 'Nana' or a standard kept pruned, use a large pot (15 gallons or more) that drains well, and give it full sun. In cold areas the pot lets you move the plant to shelter for winter, which is a real advantage where the ground is too cold.

Choose a genetic-dwarf ('Nana') or a standard cultivar held small by pruning, give it the largest practical free-draining pot (15-plus gallons) and full sun, and keep moisture even through fruiting. In cold-winter regions the pot is an asset, letting you move a frost-tender plant to shelter for the winter.

The tank keeps the lower roots wet all the time, and this drought-loving plant would rather have soil that drains freely. Use a regular pot with good drainage and water it deeply and evenly yourself.

Its reservoir keeps the lower root zone continuously wet, which works against the free drainage this drought-adapted plant prefers and raises root-rot risk.
